title: IIT Delhi alumnus' startup sues Apple for Rs 1,500 crore over NameDrop patent dispute; Seeks ban in India
summary: IIT Delhi alumnus startup sues Apple for Rs 1,500 crore over NameDrop patent dispute
detailed: A simple feature that allows iPhone users to exchange contact details by bringing two devices close to each other has become the centre of a major patent dispute between Apple and an Indian startup.
GG Technologies, a company founded by IIT Delhi alumnus Gaurav Goel in 2018, has filed a patent infringement lawsuit against Apple in the Bombay High Court.
GG Technologies' patent filings began in May 2019, while Apple announced NameDrop in June 2023.
The startup has also sought Rs 1,500 crore in damages, arguing that Apple's use of the disputed technology has affected its business prospects.
sentences: A simple feature that allows iPhone users to exchange contact details by bringing two devices close to each other has become the centre of a major patent dispute between Apple and an Indian startup.
GG Technologies, a company founded by IIT Delhi alumnus Gaurav Goel in 2018, has filed a patent infringement lawsuit against Apple in the Bombay High Court.
The startup alleges that Apple's NameDrop feature uses technology covered by its earlier Indian patent, which relates to proximity-based contact transfer.
The company, which operates the contact-sharing platform StayTouch, is seeking Rs 1,500 crore in damages.
It has also requested an interim direction requiring Apple to disable NameDrop in India through a software update, to the extent technically feasible, while the legal proceedings continue.

The case raises important questions about intellectual property rights, technology innovation and the ability of startups to protect their patents when competing with large global technology companies.
The dispute centres on Apple's NameDrop feature, introduced in 2023 as part of its contact-sharing functionality.
NameDrop allows users with compatible Apple devices to exchange contact information by bringing their devices close together.
Users can review the details they want to share and choose whether to proceed with the transfer.
GG Technologies claims that it developed a similar proximity-based contact-sharing system several years before Apple introduced NameDrop.
According to the startup, its technology was developed through StayTouch, a platform designed to make exchanging contact information easier without requiring users to manually enter details.
The company argues that Apple's NameDrop feature infringes its Indian patent, which covers a method and system for transferring contacts between nearby devices.
In its lawsuit, GG has asked the Bombay High Court to direct Apple to stop using the disputed technology in India while the matter is being examined.
The request includes disabling NameDrop through a software update, if technically possible.
The startup has also sought Rs 1,500 crore in compensation, describing the amount as a conservative estimate of the damages it believes it has suffered.
The legal dispute revolves around Indian Patent No.
546169, titled 'Method and System for Proximity-Based Contact Transfer'.
GG Technologies' patent filings began in May 2019, while Apple announced NameDrop in June 2023.
The Indian patent was granted to the startup on July 27, 2024.
The patented system describes a process through which nearby devices can identify each other, exchange relevant information and allow users to approve or reject contact transfers.
It also includes provisions for a central server to maintain contact profiles and synchronise changes.

The startup further claims that Apple's iCloud infrastructure performs functions similar to the central-server mechanism described in its patent.
However, these are allegations made by GG Technologies and have not been established as findings by a court.
The key question in the case is whether Apple's NameDrop feature uses the same technical methods covered by GG Technologies' patent.
The startup argues that both systems rely on similar processes to identify nearby devices, establish a connection and allow users to exchange contact details after giving consent.
However, the extent of the technical similarities remains disputed.
GG Technologies has submitted two expert reports to support its allegations.
These reports identify substantial similarities between the technologies, but neither expert had access to Apple's source code.
Instead, their assessments were based on publicly available information about NameDrop and the patent specifications.
This leaves several technical questions unanswered, including whether Apple uses the same device identifiers, server architecture and sequence of operations described in GG's patent.
Apple may challenge these claims during the legal proceedings.
The final determination will depend on the evidence presented before the court.
Apart from the alleged patent infringement, GG Technologies has highlighted the competitive disadvantage it faces against Apple.
The startup argues that NameDrop has a significant distribution advantage because it is integrated into compatible Apple devices.
In comparison, users need to download the StayTouch application separately to access its contact-sharing functionality.
According to GG, this difference has affected its ability to establish commercial partnerships.
The company claims that potential business partners were already being offered similar functionality through Apple's ecosystem.
To explain the difference in market reach, the startup has referred to Apple's annual sales in India crossing $10 billion.
However, this figure is being cited to demonstrate Apple's business scale and is not an estimate of revenue generated specifically through NameDrop.
GG Technologies has also submitted a chartered accountant's certificate showing that its technical development and marketing expenditure between 2019 and 2025 amounted to approximately $2.75 million.
The company is seeking Rs 1,500 crore in damages, which it describes as a conservative estimate.
It has argued that the final calculation would depend on access to information about Apple's devices and revenue.
However, the plaint does not provide an independent calculation establishing the basis for the claimed compensation.
GG Technologies says its journey with proximity-based contact sharing began before Apple's NameDrop announcement.
The dispute is not limited to India.
GG Technologies has also initiated legal proceedings against Apple in the United States.
The startup filed a patent infringement lawsuit there in April 2026.
However, the proceedings have been stayed since September while a separate investigation by the US International Trade Commission is underway.
The USITC instituted the investigation in August 2026.
A favourable finding for GG could potentially lead to restrictions on imports of devices found to infringe the relevant patent into the United States.
GG Technologies also filed another patent infringement lawsuit against Apple on November 3, 2026, involving a separate patent.
The parallel proceedings indicate that the startup is pursuing its intellectual property claims across multiple jurisdictions.
Explaining the idea behind the company, founder Gaurav Goel said that the objective was to make sharing contact information simpler and more convenient.
"When I conceived StayTouch in 2018, the idea was simple: make sharing contact information easier, faster and more intuitive," Goel said.
The founder's statement reflects the original vision behind the product, which was designed to simplify the process of exchanging contact details.
For GG Technologies, the current legal battle is also about protecting the technology it claims to have developed and patented before Apple's NameDrop launch.
The patent dispute is now before the Bombay High Court.
GG Technologies has requested the court to direct Apple to disable NameDrop in India while the case is being heard.
The startup has also sought Rs 1,500 crore in damages, arguing that Apple's use of the disputed technology has affected its business prospects.
However, the allegations are yet to be established through judicial findings.
